title: Ryokan plays
hook: Ryokan plays hide and seek with village children till after dark

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ryokan and the thief, the monk who gave away his clothes and kept the moon. Your line was I wish I could give the moon. What did you give away? Day one thousand eight.
screen: `I WISH I COULD GIVE THE MOON.`

segments.voice: Late afternoon in a village. A group of children run up to an old monk with a begging bowl and shout his name. Not to ask for a blessing. To ask him to play. He sets the bowl down. They play ball, then hide and seek, and when it's his turn to hide he crawls into a pile of straw in a field and goes perfectly still. The children search. It gets dark. They go home for supper and forget all about him. The next morning, the story goes, a farmer comes to move the straw and finds the monk still there. Shh, the monk whispers. The children will find me. Today's word: Ryokan plays.
screen: `THE CHILDREN WANT TO PLAY.` → `HE HIDES IN THE STRAW.` → `SHH. THEY'LL FIND ME.`

segments.voice: First, how the story reaches us. Like the thief story, it's a story people tell about Ryokan. Versions differ on where he hid; the monk stays the same. Second, play as practice. Ryokan's poems, as they've come down to us, keep returning to children, to a ball, to a spring day that ends too soon. Tradition says he carried a cloth handball in his sleeve. For him, playing doesn't seem to have been time stolen from practice. It was a place practice showed up: full attention, no score worth keeping, no reputation to protect. Third, still hiding. Why stay all night? Some readers hear a holy fool, a man too simple to notice the game was over. Others hear faithfulness: he gave his word to the game, and he kept it. Others hear complete absorption, so present to hiding that nobody was left inside to give up. The story doesn't choose for you. Fourth, the week behind us. It's been a week of teachers from Japan. Bassui asked who is hearing. Bankei pointed to the unborn mind, already here. Basho heard the sound of water when a frog jumped into an old pond. Hakuin, blamed for a baby that wasn't his, said is that so, and taught the butter that melts. Ryokan gave away his clothes and kept the moon. And today he's in the straw, still hiding, waiting for the children to come back.
screen: `VERSIONS DIFFER ON WHERE HE HID.` · `PLAY AS A PLACE FOR PRACTICE.` · `WHY STAY ALL NIGHT?` · `A WEEK OF TEACHERS FROM JAPAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: play, right where you are. Settle, and breathe. Then pick something small and playful: tap a rhythm on your knee, balance a pen on one finger, hum a tune, toss a balled-up sock from hand to hand. Do it with your whole attention, the way a child does when nothing else exists. When your mind starts grading how silly this is, notice that, and go back to playing. The bell holds the time.
Ryokan plays. The monk who hid in the straw for the children's game and was still hiding at dawn. Today's word.
Your line: still hiding. Today, play for five minutes, a game, a ball, a song, all the way in, as if nobody were keeping score. Day one thousand eight.

howItsDone: Ryokan's poems about children and play are read in Zen communities and in Japanese schools and homes, and his story is told as a picture of practice that includes simple joy.
